And of course your income doesn’t go up.”A political independent who typically votes Republican and has voted for Trump three times, Lnenicka said she had hoped his second term would be more like his first.“I just do not feel like it has gotten a lot better," she said..Most Americans say Iran war isn't worth fighting. About 6 in 10 Republicans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, according to the new poll, up from about half in April. “It definitely doesn’t feel like we have trended in the right direction," agreed Kristen Slaven, 41, a mental health therapist who lives in Gluckstadt, Mississippi, and typically votes Republican. She said Trump is focused on the wrong things.“Obviously wars don’t help. When they’re necessary, I understand. But our focus on renaming bodies of water and pieces of land, that’s just stupid to me when people can't feed their family," she said.“I had hoped that it would be better,” Slaven added. Some Republicans are still willing to cut Trump some slackDespite their frustration, most Republicans, 67%, say factors outside of Trump's control are more to blame for high prices.“I think inflation is a very difficult thing to tackle," said Fred Naumann, 51, a Republican and longtime Trump supporter who lives in Green Bay, Wisconsin..Iran war: Why Tehran sees Trump’s midterms as its next battlefield. Though he would like to see interest rates come down, Naumann, who works in the automotive industry, supports tariffs and the war with Iran, believing it was necessary. Overall, however, most Americans, 69%, continue to say the war has not been worth fighting, up slightly from 64% in July. Only 28% approve of how Trump is handling Iran. Americans are also unhappy with Trump's trade wars. Only about 3 in 10 U.S. adults approve of how he is handling trade negotiations with other countries, down from about 4 in 10 in March. And 64% say he has “gone too far” on imposing new tariffs on other countries, up from 58% in January.Overall, the picture is not better. Only about 3 in 10 Americans approve of how Trump is handling his job as president. And about 6 in 10 say the country as a whole is “much” or “somewhat” worse off than when he began his second term.The issue on which Trump maintains relative strength is border security, with about half of Americans saying they approve of his performance.Trump faces more blame than Biden didTrump's low grade on the economy rivals Biden’s 28% approval rating in June 2022, when there was record-high inflation during the COVID-19 pandemic. .US House votes for a third time to end Iran war. But Americans were less likely to blame Biden in the lead-up to that year's midterm elections, a sharp contrast with the solid majority who hold Trump responsible now. In October 2022, 44% of Americans said Biden’s policies were responsible for high prices, while 55% blamed factors outside of his control. Sanchez, a Republican who voted for Trump, blames him, at least in part.“I think he has a lot to do with it. This war in Iran, the tariffs that he’s placing on other countries, obviously are affecting us. Those two things are things he’s been directly involved in that directly affect the economy,” he said. “I think with Biden, a lot of the stuff was outside of his control. It was all the COVID and how that affected everything else. I don’t think that there was much that he could have done."He had high hopes for Trump's return. Now, things seem worse than under Biden..How the Iran war reshaped the global economy — and created winners and losers.Trump approval hits new low as Americans fear long Iran war.Friend and foe: Netanyahu, Iran complicate Trump’s exit from Middle East conflicts.Trump says oil firms making 'too much money' from Iran shortage
news.summary: Most Americans blame Trump for high prices as midterms approach, a new AP-NORC poll finds

news.title: “Paper Trail” Podcast: Who Is Trump’s Shadow President, Russell Vought? — ProPublica
news.text:
Description

Reporter Andy Kroll got his hands on secret tapes of a low-profile bureaucrat named Russell Vought. Turns out, as director of the Office of Management and Budget, he’s been quietly reshaping the federal government and commanding many of the second Trump administration’s biggest moves.

Editor’s Note: “Paper Trail” is produced as an audio series. If you are able, we encourage you to listen to the series. This transcript has been lightly edited for style.

Jessica Lussenhop: We’re almost halfway through President Donald Trump’s second term, and no matter where you stand on the president, it’s clear that round 2 has been very, very different than the first.

Andy Kroll: You don’t have to think hard to remember how chaotic and soap-opera-like the first Trump administration was.

Lussenhop: This is my colleague Andy Kroll. He reports on the federal government.

Kroll: Just every single day, some new, crazy new thing was happening, and it seemed like nothing really was getting done out of the White House. Compare that to the last 18 months of Trump 2.0, it’s night and day. There is a plan.

Lussenhop: In more ways than I can keep track of, the federal government has changed dramatically. The White House has ignored Congress, carried out its agenda both at home and around the world without much regard for the norms of checks and balances. Agencies like USAID have been dismantled. Others like ICE have grown explosively. And Andy says at the center of it all is one man.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, President Donald Trump: America is respected. …

Lussenhop: No, actually, not that one.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, Elon Musk: This is the chainsaw for bureaucracy!

Lussenhop: Uh, not him either.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, Pete Hegseth: The War Department is going to fight decisively.

Lussenhop: Nope.

Kroll: If you wanna understand the difference between Trump 1 and Trump 2 and why this time feels so different and so much more consequential, I think you’ve gotta look toward this guy, Russ Vought.

Lussenhop: I’m sorry, Russ who?

Kroll: Russ Vought. By staying under the radar, by not getting out in front of the president, he has more influence. It’s part of his superpower, for lack of a better way to put it.

Lussenhop: Vought — that’s V-O-U-G-H-T — he’d worked for the Office of Management and Budget during Trump’s first term. Not exactly high profile. But a lot of the things we do know about him, we know because of Andy.

Kroll: I’ve been directly reporting on him since the summer of 2024, when we got this first really juicy tip about him.

Lussenhop: The summer of 2024 was the ramp-up to the November presidential election, pitting Kamala Harris against Trump. A contact of Andy’s reached out to him and said, hey:

Kroll: We have some videos of speeches given by Russ Vought. He’s speaking to his allies, his friends, at a closed-door gala kind of event. Hasn’t been reported on. You know, you should take a look and tell us what you think.

Lussenhop: Were these speeches that were ever supposed to land in the hands of a reporter like you?

Kroll: Never.

Lussenhop: At first glance, Vought was pretty unassuming.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Russell Vought speech: When we started this organization people were very kind to us. …

Kroll: He’s balding, tortoiseshell glasses, chinos, he looks like a high school history professor, frankly. You look at him, you do not think architect of a president’s all-encompassing plan to change the shape of the American government and the course of American history. You just don’t. But then you listen to what he says.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: The stark reality in America is that we are in the late stages of a complete Marxist takeover of the country.

Kroll: And you go: “Whoa. OK. This is, this is for real.”

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: How can we possibly be in the midst of tyranny? That’s the question of this morning.

Kroll: He believes the American government is no longer a democracy, that it has been quietly taken over by these unelected bureaucrats.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: A new regime, if you will, that pays only lip service to the Constitution.

Kroll: The so-called deep state: They run the show, and that what we need is a president who is a, quote-unquote, “radical constitutionalist” to come in and put things right.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: And guess what? We have in Donald Trump a man who is so uniquely positioned to serve this role. …

Kroll: But then you hear him say:

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: We want the bureaucrats to be traumatically affected. We want— when they wake up in the morning, we want them to not wanna go to work.

Kroll: This particular comment hit me like a bag of bricks. We need to run the government in such a way that we’re gonna traumatize the people who work for it. They’re gonna be so beaten down, demoralized, that they won’t wanna get out of bed in the morning and go to work. He believes himself to be on this mission, this righteous cause.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: To dismantle and deconstruct and defund this post-constitutional regime.

Kroll: I mean at the time, I thought, this is someone who is not only much more important than I thought, but someone who is going to be an absolutely critical player in a second Trump administration if Trump were to get reelected. And of course, that is exactly what’s happened.

Lussenhop: As soon as Trump was elected — he brought Russ Vought back into the administration — to the Office of Management and Budget. Maybe that sounds like a straightforward accounting job, but that’s not the way Vought sees it. He treats it like the true seat of power. If you control the flow of money, you can effectively control the budget. If you control the budget, that’s everything.

Andy has spent the last two years following how Russ Vought operates, and how he’s reshaping the federal government in ways that will last long beyond this presidency. He’s been combing through private speeches nobody outside Vought’s circle was supposed to hear, some of which we’re going to play for the first time.

Vought’s official title is director of the Office of Management and Budget. But Andy says there’s an easier way to think about him: the shadow president.

I’m Jessica Lussenhop, and this is “Paper Trail.”

Kroll: In the movie version of the Russ Vought story that I have casted and directed and played in my mind more times than I’d care to admit, there is one moment that sets us on the course that we find ourselves on right now.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, NJ Spotlight: Chaos on Capitol Hill tonight, thousands of pro-Trump protesters clashed with police, halting the joint session to certify the electoral college vote won by Joe Biden …

Kroll: It’s January of 2021. The January 6th insurrection has just happened. People who had been loyal to the president, who were working in his own White House at the time, head for the exits.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, Fox News: Some breaking news, and I want to get your take on it. This is the first Cabinet member-level resignation. Secretary of Transportation …

Kroll: Elaine Chao, wife of Senate leader Mitch McConnell.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, NewsNation: Education Secretary …

Kroll: Betsy DeVos, who had been there the whole first term until that point, says, I’m outta here.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, NewsNation: She is now the ninth member of the administration to leave her post.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, ABC News: Lindsey Graham, who’s been perhaps the most stalwart supporter of the president … His golfing buddy. Golf whisperer … taking to the Senate floor.

Lindsey Graham: Today … all I can say is count me out. Enough is enough.

Kroll: Trump’s stock could not be lower. He’s been left for dead. And what does Russ Vought do? He pays a visit to Trump in the Oval Office. He tells Trump, I’m with you. I support you. We are gonna get through this. And I’m gonna work day and night to get you back here in the White House in four years.

Lussenhop: In the buddy comedy version of this movie, I’m really touched. Like they really had each other’s back.

Kroll: The, the Will Ferrell-John C. Reilly version. That’s right.

Lussenhop: This dynamic duo of Russ Vought and Donald J. Trump, it’s a pretty unlikely pairing.

Kroll: Russ Vought could not be more different from the commander in chief, from Donald Trump.

Lussenhop: For starters, Russ Vought grew up as an evangelical Christian.

Kroll: He comes from very modest means. There was this tragedy when he was very young where a half-sister was killed in a car accident. This death seems to spark a religious awakening for his family. They become devout Christians.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought: Let’s talk about this. I’m a Christian. I am a nationalist. And so we have a — we were meant to be a Christian nation.

Lussenhop: On the tapes Andy got his hands on, Vought talks about this.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought: Now, that doesn’t mean we’re gonna take it to crazy places.

Lussenhop: About how his religion influences his politics.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought: Like, when was the last time you had a politician, even a conservative politician, be able to appeal to the revealed truth that we have in the Bible? It never happens because we have bought into this privatized notion of faith that’s totally inaccurate.

Kroll: By the time Trump comes along, as best I can tell, Vought was wary of Trump for all of the reasons that a evangelical Christian conservative might be: the divorces, the lurid tabloid headlines.

Lussenhop: The pussy grabbing and whatnot.

Kroll: Exactly.

Lussenhop: Vought’s pull to Trump comes from the fact that he, like Trump, was a misfit in the traditional Republican Party. Which Vought realized when he spent his early career working for Republicans in Congress.

Kroll: As Vought climbs the ranks within the Republican Party. I’m talking like Tea Party era, Obama presidency, he, by his own description, is feeling more and more disillusioned with his own allies, with his fellow Republicans. They claim to be the party of small government, the party of Dickey Flatt.

Lussenhop: Dickey Flatt — a reference I was not aware of. Came from a mentor of Russ Vought’s: the Republican Senator Phil Gramm out of Texas.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, C-Span: Give a great welcome to the man Phil Gramm has made famous the world over, Dickey Flatt, from Mexia, Texas.

Dickey Flatt: Howdy.

Crowd: Howdy.

Dickey Flatt: I bring you greetings from the city of Mexia, Texas.

Kroll: Dickey Flatt was a businessman, a printer, Gramm had met on his travels through his home state of Texas.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, C-Span, Phil Gramm: He works hard for a living … and whether you see him at the PTA or the Boy Scouts or the Presbyterian Church, try as he may, he never quite gets that blue ink off the end of his fingers.

Kroll: Gramm said everything that he voted on, every program he considered, had to undergo the Dickey Flatt test.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, C-Span, Gramm: And then I’m gonna think about the millions of Dickey Flatts in this country, and I’m going to ask a simple question: Will the benefits to be derived by spending money on this program be worth taking the money away from Dickey Flatt to pay for it? And let me tell you something, there are not a hell of a lot of programs that’ll stand up to that test.

Kroll: Dickey Flatt became the face of business people, regular folk who were constantly feeling the federal government reach into their pockets and take out their hard-earned money to fund programs that didn’t work or were wasteful or whatever.

Lussenhop: Russ Vought was a Dickey Flatt-style Republican. But as he worked on Capitol Hill in the early 2000s, he thought the party had drifted way too far from its roots.

Kroll: Republican leaders: They claim to be the party of small government, and yet time and again, Republicans sign off on these mega spending bills. And they betray their own people. Vought increasingly on Capitol Hill just finds himself fighting with his own party, and it gets so bad that he leaves Capitol Hill in 2010, goes to this new offshoot of the Heritage Foundation, the big conservative think tank, working to defeat Republicans that they have deemed insufficiently conservative and to replace them with Tea Party-style, much more uncompromising, unyielding conservative candidates. What Vought comes to realize is that Trump is a vehicle. He is someone who, unlike other Republicans, wants to make dramatic change and represented the proverbial bull in a china shop.

Lussenhop: That’s why Russ Vought took a job in Trump’s bureaucracy the first time around.

Kroll: He installs himself in the Office of Management and Budget. The wonky budget plumbing of the whole federal government.

Lussenhop: Congress has the power of the purse: Members of the House and Senate set the budget. But it’s the job of the Office of Management and Budget to distribute the money that Congress allocates. The OMB writes the checks.

Kroll: Somehow, it got left out of “Schoolhouse Rock!” But it is essentially the central command board controlling the flow of money that Congress approves and how that money gets to the agencies where the stuff actually happens.

Lussenhop: Vought’s hope was he could stop the stuff from actually happening … by just refusing to write the checks. Even though he didn’t technically legally have the power to do that. Maybe he could shrink agencies — the so-called deep state — and cut government spending on stuff that he didn’t see as passing the Dickey Flatt test. Like, in Trump’s first administration, Vought had USAID — the Agency for International Development — in his crosshairs. He was also eyeballing the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, originally proposed by Senator Elizabeth Warren.

Kroll: But time and again, he keeps running into obstacles. The agencies that he’s going after, even though they’re run by Trump appointees, don’t wanna be cut in half. The lawyers say, “You know, you can’t just cancel programs or pause this funding. You can’t do these things that you’re trying to do.” And so he spends the first three years really frustrated.

Lussenhop: But what he was doing in those years was quietly experimenting with ways he could help the president get around roadblocks for his agenda: roadblocks like Congress.

Kroll: One really seminal moment is in 2019.

Lussenhop: Congress had authorized money to aid security efforts in Ukraine.

Kroll: Trump essentially tells the Ukrainian leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, you know, we’re gonna hold back these hundreds of millions of dollars in security money that we’ve said we’d give you in your war with Russia until you investigate the Bidens.

Kroll: The actual act of holding back that money, freezing money that Congress has already approved and should just head off to its destination, that happens under Vought’s watch at the Office of Management and Budget.

Lussenhop: He just doesn’t sign the check.

Kroll: Yeah.

Lussenhop: Everybody around you must be kind of screaming at you …

Kroll: Oh yeah.

Lussenhop: Send the money, and he just was like, mm, no.

Kroll: The experts at OMB, the people whose job it is to make sure that the different parts of the government function as they should, are freaking out. They’re like, you can’t do this. Uh, it’s actually illegal. It is the first time that Vought is really pushed into the spotlight. Impeachment inquiry is started. Uh, investigations are opened.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, CNN: The government accountability office says that the Trump administration broke the law by withholding that U.S. security aid to Ukraine.

Kroll: This maneuver to freeze money that Congress has approved is ultimately deemed illegal, but Vought believes the president should have the power to do that.

Lussenhop: Vought believes the president should have the power, not just to freeze money that Congress has approved, but also to redirect money they approved for one thing and spend it on something else entirely.

Kroll: The other really key battle that plays out. Remember, Trump 1.0, “Build the wall, build the wall. We’re gonna get Mexico to pay for it,” all of that sort of stuff. Trump wants billions of dollars to fund new border wall construction. Congress is like, uh, I don’t think you need that much money to do whatever it is you’re doing at the border. Even some Republicans are skeptical. What Vought ends up doing is coming up with some creative legal tinkering, declaring a national emergency at the border, to unlock, in his view, the ability for the White House to say, “Well, actually, maybe we don’t need Congress. We’re just gonna take some money from the Defense Department, and we’re gonna shift it to this border wall construction because it’s a national emergency.” Vought is rewarded for his work and his loyalty by finally getting picked to be the full-fledged director of the Office of Management and Budget. And when he is sworn in, Trump comes up to him and says this really interesting thing.

Vought: He says, “Russ, we gotta get another, another term. We’ve finally figured out how to do this.”

Kroll: You can understand why Vought feels such a sense of unfinished business when that first term is over.

Lussenhop: In the tapes, Vought talks about what came next in pretty epic terms.

Kroll: He invokes the Bible.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: In preparing for this talk, I spent a good bit of time this week in Esther.

Kroll: Specifically, the Book of Esther.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: Do you remember that story? Yes. God raised Esther, a Jew, up from nowhere to be the queen of Persia. While she is queen … an official … convinces the king to annihilate all the Jews in the empire.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: When Esther’s adopted father … asks her to beg the king to reconsider. She does what any one of us would have done with the complexities of that situation. She pauses.

Lussenhop: Russ Vought makes a big deal out of that PAUSE in the biblical story. He draws parallels to the pause in Trump’s story.

Kroll: It’s a strange thing, this four-year pause between the Trump terms. For Vought it is this really valuable period to regroup. He sets up shop in this kind of janky office where his ties are, like, hung up in the bathroom, and there’s a pigeon in the wall or the ceiling.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: We don’t invest in our offices, shall we say. We are fearless, we are faithful, and we will always be frugal, but we do need to scale. Next slide.

Kroll: And spends the next four years putting the building blocks in place to ensure that if Trump got reelected, the chaos and the division, the dysfunction, the ineptitude of the first Trump administration would not be repeated the second time around.

Lussenhop: And it’s in this pause when Vought creates his plans for a second term.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: I wake up in the morning, and I’m trying to save the country.

Kroll: Vought lays out this vision for a president and a White House that exerts a huge amount of control over the entirety of the government that you know a lot of constitutional scholars, frankly a lot of conservatives as well as liberals, Democrats, etc., find problematic because Vought is saying the president is the unitary executive, and thus everything in the executive branch should operate at his direction.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: The energy and the posture of the political capital of the administration should be to move quickly to do all they can executively, not wait on Congress for new authorities.

Kroll: The Justice Department should act at the whim of the president, the so-called independent agencies like the EPA should be much more closely attached to the agenda of the president. Anything that the president disagrees with, doesn’t align with his agenda, should be rooted out. And then the other thing he does is he oversees a bunch of work to give Donald Trump if he were to win in 2024, all of the practical, day-to-day tools to actually put this agenda into motion.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: The majority of my time right now is being spent chairing the transition portion of the Project 2025.

Kroll: The Project 2025 blueprint guide, you know, people will remember got a ton of attention.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Democratic National Convention: And this. This is Project 2025.

Kroll: People were waving it around on stage at the Democratic National Convention.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, Wall Street Journal: Project 2025 would roll back our fundamental freedoms … usher in the most conservative executive branch in modern American history … undermine our democracy, and gut checks and balances.

Lussenhop: It wasn’t just Democrats who pushed back on this … Republicans distanced themselves from it too.

Kroll: It became, honestly, an albatross around Donald Trump’s neck because it was so unpopular.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, presidential debate: I have nothing to do, as you know, and as she knows better than anyone, I have nothing to do with Project 2025.

Lussenhop: But Russ Vought was behind it.

Kroll: He writes arguably the most important chapter.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: We have detailed agency plans. We are writing the actual executive orders. We are writing the actual regulations now, and we are sorting out the legal authorities for all of what President Trump is, is running on.

Lussenhop: Sounds like doing like, doing the like boring bureaucratic work to make a lot of very unboring things happen quickly.

Kroll: Yeah. Exa-exactly.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: We are trying to build almost a shadow Office of Management and Budget. We’re trying to build a shadow office of le-legal counsel.

Kroll: Remember, in Trump 1, there were lawyers in the White House counsel’s office pushing back on some of the more extreme things Trump wanted to do.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: I don’t want President Trump having to lose a moment of time having fights in the Oval Office about whether something is legal or doable or moral.

Kroll: Vought is saying those kinds of arguments, policy disputes or frankly, moral debates about whether we should even do this or not: We’re having all of that now in the year before this election so that we’re not having them when we’re there. So that when we’re there, we’re gonna move on it.

Lussenhop: That’s after the break.

Lussenhop: At the start of Trump’s second presidency, a larger-than-life figure in the new administration dominated the news cycle: Elon Musk with a chainsaw.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, Musk: Chainsaw!

Lussenhop: The Department of Government Efficiency was going to root out waste, fraud and abuse in government agencies.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, Trump: Waste, fraud and abuse. Other than that we’re leaving it.

Lussenhop: At the same time, the words “diversity” and “women” and “Native American” were being wiped from government websites. In the background of all the in-your-face change was Russ Vought.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: Next slide. We have to be able to defund agencies that are the cause of the time that we are in.

Lussenhop: In the pause between presidencies, Vought had made a plan for this moment. But he knew that Congress and the courts weren’t going to be his only obstacles to the big project of defunding. He was going to have to convince the public.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: And that is why we are focusing so much on woke and weaponized.

Kroll: I heard him talk about how they very intentionally came up with this phrase, “woke and weaponized.”

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: How do we make spending an issue that people care about? Woke and weaponized spending, endless wars. Go ahead, next slide.

Kroll: And Vought says, “When you hear the words ‘woke and weaponized’ come out of an elected official’s mouth, you can know that that came from us.”

NEWS ARCHIVAL, John Barrasso: People feel we have an administration that is woke and weaponized against them.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, Matt Gaetz: This woke and weaponized government has to be defanged.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, Lauren Boebert: Crooked Joe’s DOJ is woke and weaponized.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, Barrasso: Woke and weaponized bureaucrats at the Department of Labor.

NEWS ARCHIVAL, Josh Brecheen: That Russ Vought has put out going after a woke and weaponized government, a government that is prioritizing the wrong things.

Kroll: Vought accused the Veteran Affairs Department of being captured by woke-ism. You know, infrastructure projects like the big Gateway project in the Northeast somehow had gotten infiltrated by DEI. It is one of the main tools in Vought’s tool kit is to slap it with the label of woke, and thus the Trump administration needed to freeze it or cancel it or stop it or, and cut it out.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: We want the bureaucrats to be traumatically affected. We want— when they wake up in the morning, we want them to not want to go to work. Because they are so — they, they are increasingly viewed as the villains. We want their funding to be shut down so that the EPA can’t do all of the rules against our energy industry because they have no bandwidth financially to do so. We wanna put them in trauma.

Kroll: “We want to put them in trauma,” is the direct quote, and I remember talking to one of these very workers who said, “Yeah, I’m, you know, I’m, I’m feeling pretty traumatized right now.” Like, if you’re Russ Vought, you’ve probably mission accomplished, at least on this piece.

Lussenhop: In the two years since Trump’s second election, Russ Vought has shrunk the quote-unquote deep state that he thinks has been antidemocratic and tyrannical. And he’s done all of this radical remaking of our government simply by … firing as many people as possible and not signing the checks.

Kroll: He has been using his powers to go to Congress and say, politely, “Hey, I know you signed a law that said that these billions of dollars should fund foreign aid and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, but actually, I want you to Control + Z that and get rid of it.”

Lussenhop: The end of the Corporation for Public Broadcasting has been a death knell for NPR and PBS stations around the country, especially in rural areas. Those cuts to foreign aid — my ProPublica colleagues reported they created a hunger crisis abroad.

Kroll: Money for, like, clean energy subsidies, Head Start, PEPFAR, the AIDS prevention program that George W. Bush put into place, money for the Department of Transportation, money for the Department of Education. Like, across the board, he is just aggressively turning off faucets everywhere he can, even though it’s not really clear that you can legally do that.

Lussenhop: And he’s also reportedly deployed the other tactic he learned in Trump’s first term — when he tried to get border wall funding — taking money Congress intended for one thing and using it for something else.

Kroll: It’s been reported that Vought has taken money, in one, in one instance meant for the Secret Service, and redirected it to help finance the new East Wing ballroom that the president is really fired up about. I mean he keeps doing things. He keeps popping up in this part of the government or that part of the government.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: But if you just said on these issues, are these all of the issues that’s needed to save the country? I would say emphatically no. There are a ton of issues that I think are first order issues.

Lussenhop: There is still plenty on Vought’s agenda.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: Low birth rate.

Lussenhop: He’s a fierce opponent of abortion rights.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: Civilian control of the military.

Lussenhop: He’s laid out plans to use armed forces to quell any domestic “riots.”

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: Central bank. We need a Fed expert, but we need a Fed expert that wants to end the Fed.

Lussenhop: Vought has led some of the White House’s attacks on the Federal Reserve.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: Artificial intelligence.

Lussenhop: And the White House is putting Al at the center of its science and tech agenda.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: Next slide.

Lussenhop: Vought’s next move, it seems, is a huge one. He is poised to expand the way the president can control the government not just at the federal level — but at the local level. The federal government gives out more than a trillion dollars to states, counties, cities and tribal governments every year.

This is money for roads and water treatment facilities and disaster response and health initiatives and schools. And the government historically has tried to do this in a theoretically nonpartisan way, by having experts review the applications.

Kroll: What Vought has proposed is to take that system, to, to, to rip out the plumbing of it and put something new in. A system overwhelmingly run by political appointees, by people who are loyal to the administration, giving more power to the federal government to take back the money, to cut off grants, to cut off these recipients if they are seen as out of line with what the White House wants them to do. You know, one expert on this stuff, described this as a plan to create this massive patronage system, where it’s all about political loyalties and relationships as opposed to the merits, as opposed to the science, as opposed to the tangible benefits to the people.

Lussenhop: When you think about all this reporting you’ve done and you, and you’re so, like, well-schooled on all his beliefs and his plans, do you have a sense of, like, a big end goal?

Kroll: I think based on everything that Vought has said I’d have to think that there is a longer-term goal to get some kind of ruling at the Supreme Court or rulings plural at the Supreme Court that reorient how the American system of government works that the commander in chief should be able to tell the DOJ what to do, tell the IRS what to do, tell the Fed what to do, and that is not how our government is conceived right now.

Lussenhop: In other words, to erode our famous system of checks and balances of power, and to concentrate it in the hands of a single person. Break and reshape things so fundamentally that, even if a Democratic president comes to power, it will take a generation to undo what Vought and Trump have done. And it seems like his ambition isn’t just to change policy: It might be to change the way Americans think about ourselves.

Kroll: Trump has put Vought in charge of implementing all of these kind of cultural-focused executive orders and initiatives. And, you know, the one that really stands out to me is this top to bottom review of the Smithsonian museums. I mean, these government institutions that tell the story of our country. Trump signs this executive order saying, we’ve got to return to a pro-American and pro-sanity version of American history. And Vought is at the forefront of that effort to change the version of American history and American culture that people see in these, in these institutions that we care so much about.

Lussenhop: It’s quite a magic trick to do all of that … through the Office of Management and Budget.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2023 Vought speech: We’re, we’re past the “Shark Tank” stage, OK? We are having an impact today, and we can have more impact today.

Kroll: He’s still as busy as ever trying to rewrite one of the fundamental jobs of what the United States government does. He is deconstructing the government, He’s thinking for the long term.

ARCHIVAL TAPE, 2024 Vought speech: You know how the story ends. … Esther is not naive. She knew the risks. She knew her very life was at stake, but she acted anyway. If I perish, I perish. If they crush me with legal bills, they crush me with legal bills. If the FBI shows up at my door, it shows up at my door. If I end up in jail, I end up in jail. If I’m slandered, I’m slandered. If I’m ostracized, I’m ostracized, but I will do my duty, and then God can take care of the results.

news.title: Most Americans blame Trump for high prices as midterms approach
news.text:
Americans are deeply frustrated with President Donald Trump's handling of the economy and rising prices, with most panning his performance and blaming his policies as higher costs threaten his party's chances in November.

A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of the Republican president's handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.

A majority, 65%, of U.S. adults now blame Trump's policies for persistently high costs more than factors outside of his control, signaling growing weariness over his aggressive use of tariffs and continued unhappiness with the war with Iran.

The dismal numbers come just weeks before midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress and while Trump is hitting the campaign trail with an aggressive schedule of rallies. But Trump — who has asked voters to pretend that he is on the ballot as he tries to bolster turnout — remains deeply unpopular, with even many Republicans faulting him for failing to deliver on promised relief.

"I was hoping it would be better or different, but it's not really good," said Robert Gault, 66, a retired factory worker from Bradford, Pennsylvania, who describes himself as a Republican.

"Our president, I thought, was going to help the country, and so far he has not really seemed to have done that with the economy or in general. He's not really done what I was hoping he would," said Gault. "He said, 'Make America Great Again.' And I have not seen him do that."

Costs drag on Trump as the economic pain keeps coming

Over the last few months, Americans have grown more worried about being able to afford basics like groceries and gas. About half of U.S. adults now say they are "extremely" or "very" concerned about being able to fill their tanks, up from 39% in July. About half are also highly concerned about being able to afford food.

Prices are "extremely exorbitant. Just the cost of everything is going up as a result of fuel," said Pedro Sanchez, 52, of Perris, California, who voted for Trump and works in law enforcement. "I used to have a lot more disposable income. I don't have that any more. It's gotten eaten up because of all these increases in the cost of everything."

Trump's current approval on the economy is a 14 percentage point drop from March 2025, just after he took office for the second time. His struggles on the issue mark a significant departure from his first term, when the economy was often a point of strength.

Trump spent much of the 2024 campaign hammering President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats, on inflation and promising to lower prices. Now, there's widespread disappointment with his performance. About 7 in 10 Americans say Trump's handling of the cost of living has been "worse than expected." That includes roughly half of Republicans, who are also broadly concerned about being able to afford groceries and gas.

"Groceries are just like kind of out of control. It seems like everything is going up," said Bethany Lnenicka, 41, who operates a small farm in Fairfax, Iowa. "It's just one thing and the next week it's another thing. It's just insane. And of course your income doesn't go up."

A political independent who typically votes Republican and has voted for Trump three times, Lnenicka said she had hoped his second term would be more like his first.

"I just do not feel like it has gotten a lot better," she said.

About 6 in 10 Republicans disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living, according to the new poll, up from about half in April.

"It definitely doesn't feel like we have trended in the right direction," agreed Kristen Slaven, 41, a mental health therapist who lives in Gluckstadt, Mississippi, and typically votes Republican. She said Trump is focused on the wrong things.

"Obviously wars don't help. When they're necessary, I understand. But our focus on renaming bodies of water and pieces of land, that's just stupid to me when people can't feed their family," she said.

"I had hoped that it would be better," Slaven added.

Some Republicans are still willing to cut Trump some slack

Despite their frustration, most Republicans, 67%, say factors outside of Trump's control are more to blame for high prices.

"I think inflation is a very difficult thing to tackle," said Fred Naumann, 51, a Republican and longtime Trump supporter who lives in Green Bay, Wisconsin.

Though he would like to see interest rates come down, Naumann, who works in the automotive industry, supports tariffs and the war with Iran, believing it was necessary.

Overall, however, most Americans, 69%, continue to say the war has not been worth fighting, up slightly from 64% in July. Only 28% approve of how Trump is handling Iran.

Americans are also unhappy with Trump's trade wars. Only about 3 in 10 U.S. adults approve of how he is handling trade negotiations with other countries, down from about 4 in 10 in March. And 64% say he has "gone too far" on imposing new tariffs on other countries, up from 58% in January.

Overall, the picture is not better. Only about 3 in 10 Americans approve of how Trump is handling his job as president. And about 6 in 10 say the country as a whole is "much" or "somewhat" worse off than when he began his second term.

The issue on which Trump maintains relative strength is border security, with about half of Americans saying they approve of his performance.

Trump faces more blame than Biden did

Trump's low grade on the economy rivals Biden's 28% approval rating in June 2022, when there was record-high inflation during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But Americans were less likely to blame Biden in the lead-up to that year's midterm elections, a sharp contrast with the solid majority who hold Trump responsible now. In October 2022, 44% of Americans said Biden's policies were responsible for high prices, while 55% blamed factors outside of his control.

Sanchez, a Republican who voted for Trump, blames him, at least in part.

"I think he has a lot to do with it. This war in Iran, the tariffs that he's placing on other countries, obviously are affecting us. Those two things are things he's been directly involved in that directly affect the economy," he said. "I think with Biden, a lot of the stuff was outside of his control. It was all the COVID and how that affected everything else. I don't think that there was much that he could have done."

He had high hopes for Trump's return. Now, things seem worse than under Biden.
news.summary:
Americans are deeply frustrated with President Donald Trump's handling of the economy and rising prices, with most panning his performance and blaming his policies as higher costs threaten his party's chances in November.



     A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of the Republican president's handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.

news.title: What to know about Illinois' 97th House District race between Jessica Dixon Heitman and Gabby Shanahan
news.text:
Appointed state Rep. Jessica Dixon Heitman, D-Plainfield, seeks election to a full term against Republican nominee Gabby Shanahan, who narrowly lost in 2024 to ex-state Rep. Harry Benton before his resignation amid sexual harassment allegations.

What’s important about this race?

This far southwest suburban district provides one of the few competitive races on Illinois’ heavily gerrymandered political map, and it’s at the center of the latest sexual harassment scandal to rattle Springfield.

Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch knew of a complaint against Benton shortly after the ex-lawmaker took office in 2023, but the speaker still directed $1.4 million to Benton’s reelection campaign.

Facing complaints from two more women, Benton resigned this summer, admitting no wrongdoing. Will and Kendall county party leaders appointed Dixon Heitman to fill his seat.

What do state representatives do?

Members of the Illinois House propose and vote on bills to become state law, advocating for resources for their districts.

Who is Jessica Dixon Heitman?

Dixon Heitman is a Democratic former statehouse media relations staffer and a public relations consultant who briefly worked as a contract employee in Benton’s office, but left after noticing “red flags” in his behavior, she has said.

She’s also a granddaughter of the late former U.S. Sen. Alan Dixon.

Who is Gabby Shanahan?

Shanahan is a Republican court-appointed special advocate for children in the Kendall County court system, and a former member of the Kendall County Board of Health.

In 2024, she lost to Benton by about four percentage points in a district that supported Kamala Harris by roughly the same margin over President Donald Trump in that year’s election.
news.author: Mitchell Armentrout

news.title: How 16 undecided voters are weighing their 2026 election options
news.text: James Morton isn’t sure which party he’s going to support in November’s elections, and he doesn’t like his options. Morton, a 67-year-old retired truck driver in Colorado, said Democrats have “gone too far to the left towards socialism,” while Republicans are “globalists” who “don’t care about the working-class people in this country.” Morton, an independent who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, is leaning toward backing third-party candidates in races for the House and the Senate this year. But he said his decision will come down to the high cost of living. “The No. 1 thing is getting the cost of things back down, inflation under control, and pretty much that’s it,” Morton said. He noted that he and his wife have been buying different groceries as they navigate high prices. Morton is among the 5% of voters surveyed last month in a national NBC News poll who said they weren’t sure which party they wanted to see controlling Congress after this year’s elections. NBC News spoke with 16 of those undecided voters as they weigh their votes this fall, some of whom declined to share their full names discussing politics. These voters feel little loyalty to either party — and many of them said that’s in part because they aren’t sure either party understands what’s important to them. Almost every one said high costs are top of mind. In the NBC News poll, 50% of voters said they wanted Democrats to win control of Congress in the midterms, while 45% said they wanted Republicans to have control. How the undecided voters in between resolve their strong, sometimes conflicting feelings could ultimately decide what Congress looks like in 2027, from who controls the majority to how many seats that party holds. Costs dominate Voters’ focus on making ends meet has been standing out in recent polling. In the latest NBC News survey, voters ranked cost of living and inflation as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption and threats to democracy. “I don’t like how expensive things are, and I don’t think anyone does,” said Aidan Valenzuela, a 19-year-old security worker in Texas, who said he hasn’t decided whom to support in his state’s hotly contested races for governor and the Senate. Joanne, a 72-year-old Vermont independent who works for a heating company, said she plans to sit out her state’s governor’s race, and she hasn’t decided whom she’ll support farther down the ballot. “I just want somebody to bring some of these prices back down,” she said. Joanne said her husband relies on multiple medications, including insulin. “It’s pretty expensive and leaves nothing for anything else.” Luke Melanson, 49, of Louisiana, who is retired from construction work, said the rising cost of groceries has changed how he shops. “I’m not eating as much. I’m eating less food because I can only afford so much,” he said. Melanson doesn’t identify with either political party, instead considering himself a libertarian, and he declined to say where he was leaning in the midterm election. But he is frustrated with both parties and wants to see new candidates emerge who can personally relate to his financial position. “I want a plumber. I want someone that ran a smaller business, like a Kroger’s,” he said. “A teacher. I take anybody that isn’t a lawyer or someone so ultra-rich that the pay gap is so far they would never understand what I’m going through.” Meanwhile, South Carolinian Darien Thompson, a 25-year-old unarmed security guard at a mall, sees gas as the biggest financial woe of the moment. The cost of his commute is only going up. “It does take a mental load when it’s like, well, it’s going to cost this much to get to work and back, and I’m only making this much,” Thompson said. It doesn’t bode well for his long-term hopes of owning a home, and he doesn’t see any current politicians stepping up to tackle the issues in a way that has earned his support. “Politicians are getting into these petty squabbles,” he said. “But it’s, like, none of us can afford houses.” Thompson doesn’t see himself voting for a Republican in November, but he’s still undecided. He has leaned Democratic before, voting for then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, but his vote this year will depend entirely on the specific candidate Democrats run in his area. Ibraham, a 42-year-old truck driver in Ohio who isn’t registered with either party, said he plans to back Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown in the Senate race in his state. Ibraham supported Harris in 2024 and said his vote this year is driven almost entirely by the surging price of diesel and a higher cost of living. “I’ve been driving for nine years. I’ve never seen anything like it. Never. Never, ever. Even during Covid, it didn’t get that high,” Ibraham said, noting that his weekly diesel costs have jumped from $2,000 to $3,500 or $3,700. “I’m spending an extra $1,500 on diesel every week. Just think about it — it’s a fortune,” he said. Down on both parties and Trump Ibraham described his support for Brown as more about opposing Republicans than endorsing Democrats, blaming the GOP-controlled White House and Congress for the current economic struggles. “It’s not about Brown,” Ibraham said of his Senate vote. “It’s just voting against the Republicans for what they’re doing. That’s it.” Other voters who were undecided but leaning toward Democrats expressed similar views, expressing caution and saying their potential support for Democrats was motivated more by reining in Trump and Republicans. Several voters — including those who backed Trump two years ago — specifically voiced concerns about Trump’s handling of the economy and the war in Iran. “I will probably support [a] Democrat this time around just so there’s some check and balances in place,” said Aaron L., a 30-year-old California independent who works in tech. He didn’t vote in 2024 while he was moving, but he said he most likely would have voted for Trump. But nearly two years into Trump’s second term, Aaron said, the economy is “a mess.” “It seems like the party, the Republican Party, just follow whatever Donald Trump says,” Aaron said. Like other undecided voters, Aaron said the economy and the war in Iran were among his top issues. Dissatisfaction with the war was high, including among Trump voters. “One of his platforms was no more useless wars, and here we are — we’re back,” said Kevin, a 35-year-old civil engineer in Massachusetts. Kevin, a Democrat, voted for Trump in 2024 hoping he would boost the economy. This year, he said, he is leaning toward supporting Republican Mike Minogue in the Massachusetts governor’s race, hoping he could shake up the state, and leaning toward backing Democratic Sen. Ed Markey for re-election. “It goes back to the checks and balances,” Kevin said of the possibility that he could split his ticket, saying he wants to see a Democratic-controlled Congress end the war in Iran. Kaleb Saracino, 21, of Nevada, doesn’t like how many resources are being poured into the Iran war or the idea that the U.S. is fighting there in behalf of Israel. He said he wants the government to cut off support for Israel, bring down costs and refocus on issues affecting everyday Americans. “The cost of groceries, the cost of gas, the cost of living have all gone up because of these endless wars,” Saracino said. Saracino knows he doesn’t want to support Trump, so he’s leaning toward the Democrats this year. But he doesn’t have warm feelings for either party. “They’re looking out for themselves, their careers, because they’re career politicians, not so much the betterment of the American people,” Saracino said about both Republicans and Democrats. Alexis, a 20-year-old college student in Florida, also expressed frustration with both parties in Washington. “They’ve made a bunch of promises that haven’t been fulfilled, and you know why? It’s because people cannot talk to each other these days. Congress is so divided,” she said. Alexis, an independent who voted for Harris in 2024, isn’t sure whom she’ll support in the Florida Senate race. She said more could get done “when we start allowing younger candidates who are more open-minded to vouching for the American people as a whole, rather than their own specific party.” Essen Zali, a 46-year-old IT consultant from Texas, voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but backed Trump in 2024 after he became frustrated with Biden during the conflict in Gaza. Now, the Iran war has again left him frustrated. “He went two steps forward with the whole war thing, and now we are all over the place,” he said. On top of that, Zali said, Trump seems focused on the wrong things. “All the construction work that was going on in Washington, that was not ever required. All the beautifications and everything, that’s secondary. The tariff war without a reason,” Zali said. “It seems like he is burning all the ships.” Connor Woodring, a 22-year-old independent from Colorado, also supported Trump in 2024. He was another voter who felt disdain for both parties. “They’re one on the same side of the same coin, basically. Republicans are the warmongering side of it. Democrats are the side that try to pull at your heartstrings,” he said. “Either way, they’re going to vote and do the same thing they’ve done for the last 50 years, so it doesn’t matter which side you vote in.” Woodring is a registered independent and doesn’t like any candidates in his area. His preference is to vote for someone not in either major party. But, he said, “there’s a lot that can happen between now and November.”

news.title: Did She Forget?' Zara Larsson Faces MAGA Backlash Over Sexyy Red's Trump Past
news.text: Zara Larsson's surprise appearance with Sexyy Red at her Los Angeles concert has drawn criticism from some social media users, who resurfaced the rapper's past praise for Donald Trump and questioned the collaboration.Sexyy Red joined Larsson onstage at the Greek Theatre on Tuesday, 29 September. Larsson's 'Ain't My Fault' incorporated elements of Sexyy Red's 'Looking For The Hoes (Ain't My Fault)' before the rapper appeared for the latter track.The political reaction is notable because Larsson has become an outspoken critic of the Trump administration and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.Why Sexyy Red's Trump Past Came UpThe controversy traces back to comments Sexyy Red made in 2023.During an October 2023 podcast appearance, the rapper said she liked Trump and wanted him 'back in office'. She also claimed Trump's popularity had grown 'in the hood', pointing to policies she believed had benefited people there. Her performances later incorporated 'Make America Sexyy Again', a play on Trump's 'Make America Great Again' slogan, including a giant red hat carrying the phrase.But Sexyy Red's political position did not remain that straightforward. By June 2024, she pushed back against assumptions that she had formally endorsed Trump, saying she was not endorsing any presidential candidate.Then, days before the November 2024 election, she publicly backed Trump's Democratic opponent. Sexyy Red posted on 1 November that she had voted for Kamala Harris and included the hashtag '#Kamala4President'.Her political timeline includes highly publicised praise for Trump followed by explicit support for Harris.Zara Larsson Took A Very Different PositionLarsson's own political statements became particularly relevant in 2026. Earlier this year, she publicly expressed support for immigrants, transgender people, abortion rights, queer people, welfare and socialism while declaring that she hated ICE.The divide became even more visible in September when the Trump White House used Larsson's 'Midnight Sun' over footage involving ICE arrests and deportations. The video carried the message 'Never-ending deportations'. Larsson condemned the use of her song, describing the video as 'dehumanizing' and expressing sympathy for the people shown in the footage.Against that backdrop, Sexyy Red appearing alongside her only days later caught the attention of some users on X.X Users Question the CollaborationOne X user responded to footage of the performance by questioning whether Larsson had forgotten Sexyy Red's political history. Another post similarly raised Sexyy Red's previous Trump comments while questioning the apparent contrast with Larsson's publicly stated politics.Those individual reactions do not establish a widespread backlash among Larsson's fanbase, but they show how the collaboration became part of an online political discussion almost immediately.Calling Sexyy Red simply a current MAGA or Trump-supporting artist would also omit important context. She praised Trump in 2023, later rejected assumptions that she had formally endorsed him, and ultimately backed Harris in 2024.There is likewise no evidence that Larsson bringing Sexyy Red onstage represented an endorsement of any of the rapper's previous political statements. The controversy instead centres on a perceived inconsistency raised by some social media users.In 2023, Sexyy Red praised Trump. In 2024, she backed Harris. In 2026, Larsson became an outspoken critic of Trump's immigration policies.Their unexpected Los Angeles performance has now brought those contrasting political moments back into the same conversation.
news.author: Clark Garret Alvarez

news.title: Jon Stewart expects Schumer, Jeffries to disappoint if the Dems win back the House and Senate
news.text:
Talk show host Jon Stewart suggested that even if Democrats win a massive victory in the midterms, a future Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-NY, and a future Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries, D-NY, will turn out to be massive disappointments.

Democrats were initially in disarray after President Donald Trump’s victory against Kamala Harris in November.

However, as Trump’s base fractured amid the Iran war and the affordability crisis that followed, Democrats are expected to win a historic victory in this November’s midterms.

On Wednesday, Stewart was asked a humorous question on his podcast about whether the downside of a Democratic midterm victory will be Schumer and Jeffries getting more “airtime.”

“Look, I think what’s going to happen is they’re going to have to f–king do something. They’re going to have to deliver,” he said. “They’re not going to be able — it will not be sufficient to make their entire personalities opposition to whatever Trump politics are; they’re going to have to have a prescription for rebalancing this economy in a smart and urgent way.

“I am not confident that is in their DNA,” Stewart continued. “I’m not confident that it’s in Schumer’s DNA, certainly, which means I’m actually hopeful he won’t be there as the leader. That they will come in and say, ‘We’re not going to go down that corporatist path again. We are going to make the changes that the American people are demanding that we make in an urgent way that is not bound by some idealized vision of what the parliamentarian might think is OK.’”

“F–k that,” Stewart said. “Like, if you are granted control, if they give you the ring, do something with it, you b—–ds.”

Fox News Digital contacted Jeffries and Schumer and did not receive an immediate reply.

Veteran GOP strategist Mary Marslender told Fox News Digital she agrees with Stewart’s take.

“I agree with Jon Stewart that both Schumer and Jeffries are not confident leaders, but that’s because their ideology is power,” she responded. “They are not the brakes that will restrain the Democratic Party from pursuing a radical agenda. Instead, they often appease the more radical members of their conference and push the party leftwards on issues like the courts, federal agencies, government spending, progressive prosecutors and immigration whenever they have the votes.

“Both men have shown little willingness to challenge the party’s more extreme factions; for example, they have said they will welcome DSA candidates who win primaries into their ‘big tent’ party,” she added. “They are not centrists; they follow the prevailing political winds within their party and will implement those policies to hold power even if those policies run counter to what the American people support.”

Former Democratic advisor Dan Turrentine argued that Stewart’s comments express the frustration Democratic voters have with party leaders.

“Voters are frustrated and angry that neither party is focused on them,” he told Fox News Digital. “We are winning because Republicans are losing, not because we are doing things well. news.title: The Democrat Who Won One Of Trump’s Strongest States Has A Bold Midterms Prediction
news.text:
ATLANTA – Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) has a bold prediction for the coming November midterm elections, one that has many in his party crossing their fingers: Democrats will win majorities in both chambers of Congress while flipping a number of gubernatorial mansions to blunt President Donald Trump’s agenda.

“I pray a lot during Trump 2.0.,” he told a crowd at Emory University’s Glenn Memorial United Methodist Church on Wednesday. He outlined exactly how he thinks his prayers will be answered — with a “full and fair election,” where Democrats “will” win the House and “will more likely than not” win control of the Senate.

His last prediction hit a little closer to home.

“We’re going to elect you governor of Georgia,” he said to the event’s moderator, former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic candidate for the Peach State’s chief executive.

“I receive that in the name of Jesus!” exclaimed Bottoms, who, if she won, would be the country’s first Black woman governor.

The duo was appearing together as part of a tour promoting Beshear’s book, “Go and Do Likewise: How We Heal a Broken Country.” The tour also gives Beshear opportunities to travel the country and make media appearances ahead of a likely 2028 presidential run.

Beshear, once considered a top contender in vice president-turned-presidential-nominee Kamala Harris’ late-in-the-election “veepstakes,” has more openly discussed mounting a bid in recent weeks.

At Wednesday evening’s gathering, Beshear reiterated much of what he said about a potential run during an earlier book tour appearance with Maryland Gov. Wes Moore. He also stood firm that, regardless of who the candidate is for the 2028 race, that person should be a Democratic governor (as luck would have it, several are prospective candidates).

Beshear also detailed a project his administration implemented to build housing, some powered by solar energy, atop old mining communities as an example of how to make Democratic inroads in a red state.

“A Democratic governor, in a Trump +31 state, is building affordable housing on top of coal mines with solar panels on the top. We can do hard things,” Beshear said to applause.

Beshear also suggested he would have a moral calling to run for the presidency.

“I don’t have any announcement today, but I will say that my commitment is to not leave a broken country to my kids or anyone else’s,” he added.

Beshear, who also chairs the Democratic Governors Association, seemed bullish that Democrats will win back the governor’s mansions in critical races like Iowa, Ohio, Nevada, and, of course, the mission-critical swing state of Georgia, where Bottoms is being exceedingly outspent by her affluent Republican opponent, businessman Rick Jackson.

“When we retake the U.S. House, we can stop this federal administration from doing more harm. But if we take the U.S. Senate, we can start undoing that harm,” he said. “But the path to 2028, the states that are actually in play, are governors races in 2026.”

news.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signs laws to protect workers from AI risks
news.text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. -- California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed laws Wednesday aimed at protecting workers from the threats of artificial intelligence, including potential job losses and workplace surveillance.

The laws ban employers from using the technology to predict a worker's emotional state by using their biometric data, require employers to send written notices to workers if AI is responsible for mass layoffs and ban employers from relying on AI to decide to fire someone. 

The Democratic governor also signed an executive order to require state agencies to continue to refer to the technology as “artificial intelligence” instead of the term “ super intelligence ” President Donald Trump recently ordered U.S. diplomats to use.

“AI should expand opportunity — not come at the expense of workers and families,” Newsom said in a statement. “As this technology reshapes the workplace, California is putting people at the center.”

He sharply criticized Trump at an hourlong event with reporters Wednesday for not passing comprehensive federal AI regulations at a time when industry leaders are warning about the technology’s risks. Trump said Tuesday that top tech leaders signed a voluntary accord to “self-police” AI development.

The governor signed a law this month requiring operators of AI chatbots to perform risk assessments before rolling them out and an executive order requiring the state to consult with experts to further improve oversight over the industry.

“We have to do a lot more in the absence of federal leadership,” Newsom said, leaving the door open for the possibility of calling lawmakers back for a special session to further tackle the issue.

The news conference came on Newsom's last day to sign or veto bills before he terms out in January. It also came weeks ahead of midterm elections that will decide control of Congress. 

Newsom involved himself early in that fight by leading Democrats last year in a redistricting battle to improve their chances of winning more House seats. He's said repeatedly that the stakes are high if his party doesn't succeed in November.

“There will not be a free and fair election in 2028 unless we take back the House of Representatives,” he said Wednesday. 

Asked if he's set a deadline for himself to decide whether he'll run for president in 2028, Newsom hedged, saying “that moment will arrive when it arrives.” 

Former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, who, like Newsom, hails from the San Francisco Bay Area, has also said she’s considering running for the job in 2028. Newsom told CNN recently that he wouldn’t run for president if she entered the race. He said the two haven't spoken since that interview aired.

Newsom weighed in on a proposal to temporarily raise taxes on billionaires that will be on the ballot in November, which he's consistently opposed. He said he respects supporters of the measure, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who are committed to addressing income inequality in the country.

“He's spot on about the balance between the rich and the poor,” Newsom said. “On this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”

Newsom's remarks came hours before a gubernatorial debate between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton.

“You're going to ask me, ‘Are you going to watch the debate?’” he said. “No.”
news.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed laws aimed at protecting workers from the risks of artificial intelligence

news.title: Fetal tissue supplier billed $765 procurement fee per organ, warns records could imply illegal sales: records
news.text: FIRST ON FOX: Newly obtained public records show Cercle Allocation Services billed a UCLA research operation a $765 procurement service fee tied to each individual liver and thymus specimen, while warning in internal correspondence that certain billing language could improperly imply the tissue itself was being sold. The records, obtained from UCLA through a California Public Records Act request made on behalf of Center for Medical Progress founder David Daleiden, include purchase orders and correspondence between the university and Cercle Allocation Services. An internal UCLA order form identifies the purchasing operation as part of the David Geffen School of Medicine’s Division of Hematology-Oncology and references the "Mouse Core." UCLA redacted the names and other identifying information of researchers from the record. The records reviewed by Fox News Digital do not establish that UCLA or its researchers, procurement personnel or other employees engaged in illegal or unethical conduct with the transactions. 'DRUG-DEALING' NETWORK SHIELDED BY BLUE STATES TARGETED IN SCOTUS CHALLENGE One UCLA purchase order lists seven individually numbered liver and thymus specimens at a $765 unit amount apiece, totaling $5,355. Another lists five specimens from Aug. 18, 2023, each carrying the same $765 amount, for a total of $3,825. Additional purchase orders reflect the same per-specimen amount. Cercle objected to the purchase orders’ tax treatment and asked UCLA to reissue them, telling the university that the charges reflected procurement services and that sales tax should not be applied. Cercle said tax language could improperly imply that the specimens themselves were being sold. Cercle does supply human fetal tissue for biomedical research. Peer-reviewed scientific literature has identified the company as the source of human fetal liver tissue used by researchers, providing independent evidence of the type of procurement business described by CMP. SUPREME COURT UNANIMOUSLY SLAPS DOWN BLUE STATE TARGETING PRO-LIFE GROUP CMP identified the liver and thymus specimens in the UCLA purchase orders as fetal tissue. Fox News Digital has not independently verified that the tissue associated with these specific purchase orders was fetal. The purchase orders identify the organs by type, sample number and date but do not describe them as fetal. The records do not establish that the payments were illegal. Cercle characterized the money as fees for procurement services rather than payments for the tissue itself. But correspondence shows the company was particularly concerned about how those payments were described. "The overriding issue is the use of terminology that we must not use due to their improper implication that we are selling taxable items, which we are not," a Cercle accounts manager wrote in September 2023. "Due to the nature of our business, we must be very careful and clear that we invoice fees for our procurement services." The same email said notations referring to sales tax would imply Cercle was "selling the items received," which the company said were "illegal to sell." Cercle instead instructed UCLA that purchase orders should authorize payment for its services while tying individual sample numbers and dates to a unit amount of $765. The correspondence shows UCLA subsequently prepared revised purchase orders after Cercle objected to the tax language. One Cercle email said a July invoice totaling $5,355 for procurements on three dates had already been "processed and paid." The company also asked UCLA to replace other purchase orders containing tax language, including one covering five procurements from Aug. 18 worth a combined $3,825. Federal law prohibits knowingly acquiring, receiving or otherwise transferring human fetal tissue for "valuable consideration," if the transfer affects interstate commerce, while allowing "reasonable payments" associated with transportation, implantation, processing, preservation, quality control or storage. The records reviewed by Fox News Digital do not establish that Cercle or UCLA violated that prohibition. Daleiden contends the documents raise questions about whether the uniform $765 charges represented permissible reimbursement for procurement-related costs. HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS He pointed to the uniform $765 amount UCLA assigned to individual specimens on the purchase orders, including multiple organs listed on the same date. Daleiden told Fox News Digital he believes the structure raises questions about whether the payments reflected the procurement-related costs permitted under federal law. Documents reviewed by Fox News Digital do not contain Cercle’s invoices or underlying cost calculations and do not establish whether the $765 amount exceeded reasonable procurement-related expenses. Daleiden also said UCLA did not produce Cercle’s invoices in response to the public records request. The May 2025 request sought the original and most recent materials associated with UCLA IRB No. 11-002504 and records and communications from 2023 forward between the authors of a specified UCLA study and Advanced Bioscience Resources or Cercle. The request covered records, including emails, text messages, notes and fetal tissue logs. UCLA later said its departments had completed their search and that the September 2026 production represented the final batch of non-exempt responsive records. The university said it redacted certain researcher identities because of concerns about threats and harassment involving sensitive research. Records also show the UCLA-Cercle relationship continued into 2025. A February 2025 Cercle ticket involving UCLA was titled "Liver and brain." Cercle responded March 3 that it had been "unable to fulfill your request today" and canceled the ticket. The records do not specify that the requested tissue was fetal or establish that any brain tissue was ultimately procured or transferred. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Daleiden has spent years investigating fetal tissue procurement after CMP released undercover videos involving Planned Parenthood officials in 2015. His recording operation later became the subject of a California criminal case. Kamala Harris’ office opened the investigation while she was California attorney general. Charges were later filed under Attorney General Xavier Becerra. In April 2026, a California judge dismissed the final charge and expunged the case. The records reviewed by Fox News Digital do not establish that the UCLA-Cercle transactions violated federal law. UCLA and Cercle have not been accused or charged by authorities with illegal conduct in the transactions reflected in the public records obtained by CMP. UCLA and Cercle Allocation Services did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.
news.summary: Records obtained by David Daleiden’s Center for Medical Progress show UCLA purchase orders tied $765 procurement service fees to individual liver and thymus specimens

BILL CLINTON REVEALS HOW HE FEELS ABOUT UPCOMING MIDTERMS AFTER SOCIALIST VICTORIES "[There is] no greater problem solver in that respect than Bill Clinton, in my mind. Master of his craft. Next-level," Newsom said. The California governor's embrace of Clinton also comes as he navigates an evolving Democratic Party, where democratic socialist figures have gained prominence alongside the more moderate political tradition Clinton once represented. The governor made it clear he does not associate himself with the Democratic "establishment," instead casting himself as a political "disrupter." "I’m notoriously a disrupter at heart," he told Vanity Fair. "I’ve never been for the status quo. Quite the contrary. I have a record that consistently challenges the status quo, and I tend to take risks to a degree that few elected officials do." NEWSOM TELLS DEMOCRATS TO BE IN THE 'ADDITION NOT SUBTRACTION' BUSINESS WITH SOCIALISTS Newsom, who said he won't run in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris does, also discussed a 36-page book he is writing, full of policy ideas for what he calls Project 2029, a governing framework modeled in name after MAGA's Project 2025. This is just policy, not narrative, the kinds of things we need to do: zoning reform, corporate tax, junk-fee stuff, new domestic strategies and tariffs, preschool things, a cap on childcare, family leave, paid sick leave, child tax credits, industrial decarbonization, anti-monopoly stuff, immigration, whistleblower protections." "Newsom’s challenge will be authentically casting himself as a disrupter when he has spent decades as part of the California political establishment." Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff agreed with Friednash, arguing that Clinton understood the importance of putting the country’s necessities over those of activists or party leaders, an instinct he says Newsom is "clearly trying to learn."
