news.title: Tiffany in Striking Distance of Flipping Wisconsin After Break With Trump
news.text: A Marquette Law poll released on Wednesday shows that the race between Republican Representative Tom Tiffany and Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley for Wisconsin governor is a statistical tie, as Tiffany has broken with President Donald Trump recently on beef imports, renaming Lake Ontario, data centers and more. The poll shows that Crowley has 49 percent of the vote among likely voters, compared to Tiffany's 46 percent and 5 percent are undecided. Crowley has 46 percent of the vote among registered voters compared to Tiffany's 45 percent, while 9 percent are undecided. The margin of error for likely voters in the poll is 4.8 percent and among registered voters is 4.3 percent. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during midterm elections. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. The swing state's gubernatorial seat is currently held by incumbent two-term Democratic Governor Tony Evers. Both Republicans and Democrats are keen on taking the seat after Evers announced his retirement. When reached for comment, Crowley's campaign sent Newsweek a statement regarding the new poll saying, "We've seen unprecedented spending from Trump-aligned billionaires, with three of them putting nearly $10 million into Tom Tiffany's campaign and outside groups like Richard Uihlein's super PAC and the Koch network adding more than $15 million more, and Wisconsinites are still choosing David Crowley because they know David gets it and has their back," Campaign Manager Garren Randolph said. "We're holding strong, but nobody should mistake a lead for a finish line, because these corrupt billionaires will stop at nothing to buy this election. Tom Tiffany isn’t running to serve the people of Wisconsin, he’s running to serve the billionaires, and we’re going to make sure every voter knows it now ‘til November 3rd.” In an email to Newsweek on Wednesday, Tiffany responded to the poll saying: "The more voters learn about David Crowley’s tax-hiking record, the more they’ll see how wrong he is for Wisconsin. He’s raised taxes every year as Milwaukee County Executive, introduced legislation requiring taxpayers to pay for tampons in boys’ public-school bathrooms, supports making you pay for benefits for illegal immigrants, and flies to California to raise money with Kamala Harris. David Crowley wants more of your paycheck. I’m running to give more of it back. I’ll return the $3 billion surplus, lower property taxes, and cut income taxes by 10% for working families." What To Know The new poll shows a slightly closer race compared to last month among likely voters when Crowley secured 49 percent compared to Trump-endorsed Tiffany's 44 percent. The race however was tied last month at 44 percent for both candidates among registered voters. Compared to last month's poll, Tiffany's support has risen 4 points among Republicans while Crowley's Democratic support dropped 2 points. Crowley's support among independents fell 11 percentage points, Tiffany secured a 2 percent bump with the group and the percentage of independents who are undecided rose by 8 points. Crowley's favorability in the poll is 31 percent compared to an unfavorable rating of 44 percent. Tiffany's favorability is 39 percent compared to a 45 percent unfavorable rating. The poll also highlights that Trump's approval rating sank to 38 percent and his disapproval rating is now at 60 percent. In last month's poll the president's approval rating was 40 percent compared to a 59 percent disapproval rating. Democrats are hoping to capitalize on Trump's dropping approval ratings in state and national polls as the midterm elections are less than five weeks away. The president's overall approval and ranking on key policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are flagging affordability concerns. The poll was conducted from September 16-23, 2026, among 843 registered voters in Wisconsin and 692 likely voters. Tiffany Breaks With Trump Tiffany broke with Trump recently on a slew of issues. Last month Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America." The move sparked new diplomatic tensions in the already growing rift between Canada and United States amid trade negotiations. “I believe the Great Lakes are the Great Lakes and should stay Lake Superior, Lake Michigan, Lake Ontario — I mean, unless you’re suggesting we name Lake Michigan, Lake Wisconsin,” Tiffany said, according to Wisconsin Public Radio. The Wisconsin Republican also separated his stance from Trump on a growing midterm concern--data centers. The president has touted artificial intelligence in the past and even rebranded it "super intelligence" on Tuesday, saying that AI is a "fake word." The administration has been an advocate for states and communities to welcome the centers as well as pushing for the U.S. to grow its capabilities on artificial intelligence. Tiffany has said that "we should end all subsidies for data centers. These are some of the wealthiest companies in the world, and the people of Wisconsin should not be subsidizing them," according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel last month. In an interview earlier this year with PBS Wisconsin, Tiffany called data centers "exciting new technology" while adding in part, "I think we need to make sure on the energy side of it that we do not harm existing ratepayers, so residential ratepayers and manufacturers." Trump recently announced a plan to waive tariffs on imported beef to help lower prices of the grocery store staple for Americans at home. Tiffany reacted last month saying he was standing with Wisconsin farmers who shouldn't be penalized "by having beef that comes in from other countries," the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported. What Other Polls Show A Platform Communications poll showed Crowley up 4 points with 48 percent compared to Tiffany's 44 percent. The poll surveyed 500 likely voters from August 12 to 13, 2026, and had a margin of error of 4.4 percent. An RMG Research poll commissioned by the Institute for Reforming Government, showed Crowley had 46 percent compared to Tiffany's 43 percent. The poll surveyed 800 Wisconsin registered voters from July 20–24, 2026, and had a margin of error of 3.5 percent. The Cook Political Report currently rates the race as a toss-up. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: The swing state's gubernatorial race is currently rated a toss-up by Cook Political Report as election day nears.

news.title: MAGA podcasters are abandoning the president... and a 'new Trump' is emerging
news.text:
MAGA podcasters are abandoning the president... and a 'new Trump' is emerging

Sign up HERE to our DC Insider newsletter - your guide to what's rocking Washington, rattling the White House and setting tongues wagging on the Hill

By CHARLIE SPIERING, US POLITICAL REPORTER

Published: 23:35 BST, 30 September 2026 | Updated: 23:37 BST, 30 September 2026

Add us as a preferred source

The army of influencers and podcasters who boosted Donald Trump's 2024 presidential comeback are shifting their focus to other topics as the midterm elections approach.

'I definitely have been talking about Trump less,' one MAGA podcaster told the Daily Mail. 'He doesn't primarily drive the news anymore in a sense, at least at what goes viral.'

MAGA content creators on Instagram, Facebook and TikTok have pivoted away from Trump because of changing algorithms and topics that go viral.

'I mean, we talk about what's viral. It's not like an active choice to ignore Trump, it's just trend-following,' one MAGA digital creator told the Daily Mail.

A Wall Street Journal article cited data from an artificial intelligence podcast tracker that mentions of Trump's name per hour fell nearly 70 percent from the peak of the 2024 election.

Daily Wire podcaster Michael Knowles told the Daily Mail that he continues to talk about Trump, but admits the midterms are becoming more of a part of the conversation. 

So who is the new Trump? Democrats like Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico are increasingly becoming part of the daily discussion instead. 

'I talk about Trump every day with some honest criticism, you know, and with a lot of praise, but I'm also now talking about El-Sayed and Talarico,' he said. 

The switch, he noted, was partially because of the Republican campaign messaging but more importantly from the president himself.

Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is getting more attention from MAGA Republicans for previous 'woke' views on sex and gender

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed campaigned with former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris together in Michigan, sparking Republican mockery for her comments

Daily Wire podcaster Michael Knowles noted that Trump himself is placing more Democratic candidates in the political conversation because of their left-wing views

'Nothing about Trump has changed, but Trump himself is telling us to go out there and focus on all these crazy Democrats,' Knowles said. 

'Talarico should be honored that he has achieved one of the president's nicknames, as Mr Tala-freako.'

Talarico dismissed Trump's nickname for him as 'corny' but added he was 'grateful' to the president for the nickname, which his campaign put on T-shirts and sold to supporters. 

Talarico and El-Sayed have already developed their own online ecosystem of supporters, prompting more MAGA figures to react.

Talarico has about 2.5 million followers on Instagram, 345,000 on X, and over 2 million followers on TikTok. El-Sayed has around 1.7 million followers on Instagram, 300,000 followers on X, and 938,000 followers on TikTok.

Republicans are also spending millions to remind voters of both men's radical views.

Videos of Talarico's comments about stating there were 'six' genders, that God was 'non-binary,' professing his love for 'trans kids,' and announcing he would make his campaign consume less meat went viral, prompting a response from influential podcasters and content creators. 

Likewise, El-Sayed once defended an attack on a Michigan synagogue, professed a desire to ban fireworks, supported defunding the police, replacing the Second Amendment with the right to health care, and even questioned the ethics of football.

That kind of content is irresistible for podcast hosts, one strategist noted, providing a conservative audience with an appropriate level of outrage and humorous disbelief that could inspire Republicans to vote. 

James Talarico has earned mockery for many of his past comments prior to his Senate campaign

Abdul El-Sayed has also fueled political controversy for campaigning with Democrat socialist podcaster Hasan Piker

White House crisis as Trump aide Natalie Harp takes control and causes most humiliating blunder yet

Frequently, political audiences get distracted from the midterms and jump to the conversation of who will be the next presidential nominee, podcast hosts and influencers said.

That sparked months of speculation surrounding whether Vice President JD Vance would be challenged by Secretary of State Marco Rubio for the 2028 nomination.

'There's been a major shadow war over '28,' Knowles said, even as he called the idea 'preposterous' because Rubio had already endorsed Vance for president if he decided to run.

Those online debates would continue, sources told the Daily Mail, especially if prominent influencers were hired by campaigns and special interests to promote a specific candidate.

Other Republicans who could enter the viral 2028 conversation would likely be soon-to-be former Florida Republican governor Ron DeSantis or Texas Senator Ted Cruz, sources predicted. 

Even long-shot protest candidates like Kentucky Representative Thomas Massie could build an online following from a small but vocal group of creators who are disillusioned with Trump. 

Other podcast hosts are pivoting away from President Trump and the 2024 election because their shows were never entirely focused on politics. 

Other popular comedian podcast hosts Joe Rogan and Theo Von were never serious Trump supporters, one strategist noted, but 'Trump curious,' which prompted them to host him on their show. 

'They've always been critical of the president, and I anticipate that they'll remain critical,' a Republican digital strategist told the Daily Mail.

Vice President JD Vance appeared on the Joe Rogan Experience podcast in July

A growing number of MAGA podcasters are pushing Secretary of State Marco Rubio to run for president against Vice President JD Vance

Creators and podcasters were also pulled away from Trump into more pressing cultural debates, such as the Lindsay Clancy trial. 

At another point before the election in 2024, podcasters and influencers were swept into a debate about higher costs, grappling with a world where a burrito could cost as much as $20.

Trump officials viewed those conversations as unhelpful to the president's midterm argument, sources told the Daily Mail, but they waited out the debate until it changed.

Some MAGA influencers and creators told the Daily Mail that many prominent figures who had built online platforms on the popularity of the president had now been drawn to pursuing other interests.

'They care less about winning elections and they are more interested in lining their pockets,' one Republican digital strategist told the Daily Mail. 'They're just gonna go wherever the money goes.'

MAGA influencers are now engaging in debates over Flock cameras, data centers, artificial intelligence and solar power.

'I think that the whole space has been corrupted. I don't think you'll ever reach the heights of what Trump did organically in 2024 again,' the strategist said.

Conservative podcasters and consultants also conceded that there were few Republican candidates running in 2026 inspiring enough to garner the kind of attention that the podcast and online community gave Trump two years ago.

Knowles singled out young freshman Texas Congressman Brandon Gill as a 'rock star' but conceded that he would never compete with someone like Trump.

'There's just no comparing even the very best politicians to Trump. Trump is just an American ritual,' Knowles said. 'He is a global celebrity entrepreneur that only comes around once in a century.'

Trump advisor Alex Bruesewitz, who worked on his presidential campaign to introduce him to top influencers, agreed.

'The president will still dominate the internet even when he's not the president. He's at a completely different level than any other politician when it comes to an online presence,' he told the Daily Mail.

news.summary: The army of influencers and podcasters who helped power Donald Trump's 2024 presidential comeback have suddenly pivoted away from him.

news.title: Trump Appears to Hide Brutal Polling Numbers in Truth Social Post — as Prez's Approval Rating Continues to Suffer
news.text:
President Trump has been accused of hiding his actual polling numbers after sharing a 43-second CNN clip on Truth Social that highlighted his continued strength among MAGA Republicans, omitting the rest of the analysis of his standing among other Republicans and independent voters, RadarOnline can report.

The clip featured CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten discussing MAGA support.Trump’s Republican Approval Has Declined"In the 2024 election versus Kamala Harris, he got 99 percent of the MAGA GOP vote – perhaps surprisingly, I might have thought it'd be 100 percent, but it was 99 percent," Enten said on Sunday, September 27. "Compare that to his approval rating now with the MAGA GOP. It's 98 percent; there’s been no real decline in MAGA support."

In the full segment, Enten said Trump’s approval rating among Republicans overall stood at 80 percent, a drop of 14 points from 2024 levels. 

"His approval rating now is 80 percent. So, in fact, there has been a decline in the support for Trump among Republicans. It's a decline of 14 points."

Enten compared the figure with those of previous Republican presidents at similar points before their second midterm elections. He said Ronald Reagan registered 93 percent, George W. Bush 82 percent and Dwight Eisenhower 81 percent.Inflation and Gas Prices Emerge as Issues"Donald Trump is no better than the other two right here," Enten explained. "It's within a margin of error, but technically speaking, he's in the worst shape. He's just at 80 percent among Republicans at this point."

The share of Republicans who strongly approve of Trump has also fallen, Enten said, from 71 percent at the beginning of 2025 to 47 percent. "That is a decline of 24 points," he noted.

On fuel and gas prices, Enten said Trump’s net approval had fallen from 51 points in June 2025 to minus 12 points. 

"Minus 12 points. That is Trump is underwater," the expert explained.Non-MAGA Republicans Pull Away of TrumpThe majority of Republicans still planned to vote Republican, but the CNN commentator said even a decline in support could matter in closely divided races.

Enten said more than 10 percent of non-MAGA Republicans were supporting Democratic candidates, citing a Fox News poll that put the figure at 14 percent. 

He also said Democrats were six points more likely than Republicans to say they were certain to vote in 2026. 

Among pure independent voters, Enten said Trump won by 15 points over Harris in 2024, but his current net approval rating stood at minus 71 points. 

"That's an 86-point difference. That is a huge difference."Trump’s Numbers Among Independent VotersEnten said Trump had been trusted more than Harris to handle the economy among pure independents by a 22-point margin in fall 2024, while his current net approval on the economy was minus 77 points. 

On gas prices, Enten said only 8 percent of pure independent voters approved of Trump’s handling of the issue, while 92 percent disapproved.

According to the news network, Trump aides have expressed doubts about GOP chances in the midterms.
news.summary: Trump shared a 43-second CNN clip showing strong MAGA support while the full segment examined declining approval among Republicans and independent voters.

news.title: Gavin Newsom whines that Joe Rogan is 'too chicken' to have him on show while begging for other podcast invitations
news.text:
Gavin Newsom has revived his one-sided feud with Joe Rogan by once again questioning the podcaster's masculinity.

Newsom, 58, sarcastically branded the 59-year-old podcaster a 'tough guy' during a wide-ranging interview with Shelby Church over the weekend.

The governor had just finished telling the 31-year-old YouTuber how he viewed Rogan as a 'bullsh*t artist' afraid of real conversations.

Newsom has been clamoring for a spot on the Joe Rogan Experience for nearly a year.

Church paved the way for the exchange after pointing out the 'interesting' role podcasts played in the 2024 election.

'Would you go on any of these podcasts like Joe Rogan or Call Her Daddy or any of those?' she asked, seemingly unaware of the steady stream of Newsom's X posts demanding almost exactly that.

'I mean, you’re bringing up Rogan,' Newsom said, before circling back to Cooper later. 

'I’ve long prided myself for reaching out to the people I disagree with,' the potential presidential candidate continued. 'The problem with Rogan is he won’t have me on.'

Newsom claimed the reason was Rogan was reluctant 'to be confronted with the bullsh*t that he spews, particularly in the political sense.' 

'He’s a bullsh*t artist, in political terms,' he maintained.

The audience and Church silently processed the remarks, allowing a noticeably serious Newsom to add: 'Sorry. He just is.'

The rant, however, continued.

Newsom claimed he was still 'happy to confront' Rogan.

'But he won’t do it.

'Now, I’m not even interested.'

Newsom said Rogan had lost his chance after 'bashing me on a weekly basis' for the past two years. Rogan most recently criticized Newsom as a 'cardboard cut out of a person' back in April.

The 'feud' began during a July 2023 taping of the Joe Rogan Experience, when Rogan billed Newsom as a 'terrible' politician and a 'con man' for his far-left approach to crime and homelessness.

'It’s f***ing madness. There’s so many businesses that are closing down, they don’t want to be a part of it anymore,' Rogan said at the time.

He went on to endorse Donald Trump the following year, just days before the election. Trump appeared on the Joe Rogan Experience as well, before his win over Kamala Harris.

Within a year, Newsom was tweeting out at Rogan claiming he was 'too chicken to have me on his show.' 

Days later, Rogan was asked about having Newsom on by Andrew Schulz, one of the 'man-o-sphere' comics widely credited with helping Trump win. Schulz joked: 'There is a fun version where you just do it and cook him, you know?'

'He'll cook himself. I mean, that seems to be already happening,' an unconvinced Rogan responded, panning Newsom's recent X strategy that parodies Trump.

'It's just stupid. It's like, this is a bad strategy. 

'Like, I probably would have had him on. But now I'm like, no, what are you doing?'

'Well done, tough guy,' Newsom told his and Church's audience Saturday while offering a sarcastic round of applause. The two were on-stage for a YouTube In Session event, which surrounded issues in the major cities of the Golden State. 

'I mean, obviously there's some anxiety and insecurity around it, for him. Cause it's threatening,' he told Church. 'Cause I will call him on the bullsh*t.' 

The California governor also called Rogan a 'chicken' on July 21, complaining in an X post how the podcaster still won't 'have [him] on' the Joe Rogan Experience

The governor's press team launched a similar broadside in May, writing in all-caps (a la Donald Trump): '"Little Guy" Joe Rogan is too scared to have me on, but he wont stop talking about me.'

'He is obsessed with my "good looks."' 

The month before, the same team wrote in all caps: 'Joe "Little Guy" Rogan is too chicken to have me on his failing podcast because he know (sic) I'd crush him, so he takes cheap shots from the peanut gallery as he gets relegated to irrelevancy. 

'All talk, no action. I'm ready when you are, "Little Guy." Or keep hiding!!!!' 

Rogan, meanwhile, welcomed Vice President JD Vance to his show in July. Many have pegged Vance as the likely pick for the GOP nomination.

Both Vance and Newsom have yet to formally declare a run for the White House.
news.summary: Newsom, 58, sarcastically branded the 59-year-old podcaster a 'tough guy' during a wide-ranging interview with Shelby Church over the weekend.
news.author: Alex Hammer,Editor

news.title: James Talarico is Outraising Ken Paxton in Texas’ Republican Strongholds
news.text: Some of the richest traditionally Republican neighborhoods in Texas have given more money to a Democrat this year than to the GOP nominee for the Senate. According to an analysis of Federal Election Commission records by reporters at The Houston Chronicle, Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico is outperforming Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in fundraising in ZIP codes that have previously backed President Donald Trump. The fundraising numbers come as Texas has surged to the forefront as a key state in the battle to control the Senate. Democrats are hoping to win a Senate seat in the Lone Star State for the first time since 1988 by capitalizing on Trump's low polling numbers. In University Park, a town that sits entirely inside a district that Trump carried by more than 5 points in 2024, Talarico has raised $214,296, more than 18 percent more than Paxton's $181,656 through June 30. The town represents the second-largest source of individual contributions to Paxton's Senate campaign of any ZIP code in the country. The fundraising numbers there are not an isolated result. Across 11 different ZIP codes in four metropolitan areas that fall inside state House districts Trump won in 2024, Talarico raised about $1.3 million from individual donors, compared with roughly $422,000 for Paxton. Newsweek reached out to the Talarico and Paxton campaigns for comment Wednesday. The Chronicle analysis mapped itemized individual contributions to each campaign by the ZIP code in which the donor reported. The widest gaps are in The Woodlands, a community north of Houston. Across the four ZIP codes covering the area and the suburbs around it, Talarico raised $238,622 to Paxton's $39,281. In 77381, at the center of The Woodlands, the split was $98,103 to $19,247. In 77386, covering Spring and Imperial Oaks, it was $68,076 to $4,476. West Houston runs the same way. Talarico raised $255,116 in 77024, the ZIP code for the Memorial Villages, against $60,643 for Paxton. In 77079, farther west along Memorial Drive, he raised $98,189 to Paxton's $10,405. In the Katy and Richmond suburbs, Talarico raised $152,557 across two ZIP codes, compared with $50,228 for Paxton. In 75230, which covers part of North Dallas below Interstate 635, Paxton raised $77,116, compared with $270,286 for Talarico. The Dallas suburb Highland Park remains Paxton's single best ZIP code in the country, at $211,701. Talarico Raising Money In Trump Districts The money is moving to Talarico through parts of Texas that had previously had a Republican grip, according to the Chronicle analysis. The four Woodlands ZIP codes where Talarico has outgained Paxton sit entirely within House District 15, which Trump won handily—62.8 percent to 35.8 percent—over Kamala Harris in 2024. Montgomery County as a whole gave Trump about 72 percent of its vote. The Memorial ZIP codes sit almost entirely inside House District 133, which Trump carried 52.4 percent to 45.4 percent. The Katy and Richmond ZIP codes fall in House District 26, which he won with 56.3 percent. Election results are not reported specifically by ZIP code, so the closest official measure is the state House district each ZIP code sits in. The Texas Legislative Council publishes both those results and the share of every ZIP code's population inside each district. Highland Park and University Park sit entirely within House District 108, along with part of northern Dallas and about 76 percent of ZIP code 75230. Trump won that district with 51.7 percent to Harris's 46 percent, according to the Legislative Council's official district report. The president won Texas easily in 2024, topping Harris by more than 13 percent of the vote. Despite the gains in Republican areas, Talarico's largest fundraising hauls still come from places that voted against Trump. The Democrat's best ZIP code in Texas is 78746, covering West Lake Hills and neighborhoods west of Austin, where he raised $584,863 to Paxton's $145,365. That ZIP code is 92 percent inside a House district that Harris won 69 percent to 28.6 percent. In Houston's 77019, which includes River Oaks, Talarico raised $429,975; the ZIP code did not rank among Paxton's top 10 nationwide, and his tenth-largest brought in $72,318. Fourteen Months of a Flat Line The gap between the two campaigns did not grow wider in a single quarter. It came as Paxton's fundraising stalled while he fought longtime Senator John Cornyn for the Republican nomination. Paxton raised about $2.9 million in the second quarter of 2025, the first full quarter of his campaign. He then raised $1.3 million in the third quarter, $1.1 million in the fourth, and $2.2 million in the first quarter of 2026. His numbers did not move until the primary was settled. Paxton won the May 26 runoff against Cornyn and went on to report more than $9 million for the April-through-June quarter, the best of his campaign. Talarico entered the race on September 8, 2025, and raised $6.2 million in his first three weeks. He raised $7 million in the fourth quarter of 2025, $27 million in the first quarter of 2026 and $31.6 million in the second. Through June 30, Talarico's campaign reported raising $68.6 million and spending $47 million, leaving $21.5 million in the bank. Paxton's two committees reported $9.2 million raised, $7.5 million spent and $1.76 million on hand. Paxton Reportedly Has Blamed Trump for Sagging Numbers The fundraising analysis comes as reports emerged that Paxton pointed the finger at Trump for being a drag on the ticket. At a private fundraiser in Washington last Thursday, Paxton was asked whether Trump had hurt the campaign. Paxton said the Republican convention the president staged in Dallas on September 9 and September 10 "dropped our numbers," according to a recording obtained by The New York Times. He said everyone's numbers had fallen and described the party's current position as not good. The recording was made by someone who attended the event and opposes Paxton's campaign, and was then given to the Times. Three other attendees confirmed to the paper that Paxton was present, and two recalled the question being asked of him. Nick Maddux, a senior adviser to the Paxton campaign, called the reporting "manipulated nonsense." He said the campaign's most recent internal polling put Paxton three points ahead and that its numbers had improved since early September. Trump has publicly said that the Dallas event helped Paxton a great deal. What the Most Recent Polling Shows Most public polling of the Texas Senate race continues to show Talarico ahead, although the margins are narrow. Of eight September surveys, six put Talarico ahead by one to six points. One found the race tied, while another, sponsored by Paxton's campaign, gave him a three-point lead. The latest poll, conducted by Pulse Decision Science from September 24 to September 27, surveyed 800 likely voters and found Paxton at 48 percent and Talarico at 45 percent, with 4 percent undecided. The poll was sponsored by Paxton's campaign. Its three-point margin matches the internal figure Maddux cited in dismissing the fundraiser recording. Stratus Intelligence found a 48-48 tie among 865 likely voters surveyed from September 22 to September 24 for Texans for a Conservative Majority, a Republican group. Like the Pulse poll, it was sponsored by a Republican client. Among the nonpartisan surveys, Talarico has maintained a lead. Marist University surveyed 1,139 registered voters from September 17 to September 20 and found Talarico ahead 50 percent to 44 percent, his largest lead of the month. Emerson College, polling for Nexstar, found him ahead 47 percent to 46 percent among 1,000 likely voters surveyed September 12 to September 14. The New York Times includes Marist and Emerson among its select group of pollsters. Other September surveys showed narrower leads. Slingshot Strategies, polling for Texas Public Opinion Research, found Talarico ahead 49 percent to 44 percent among 1,007 likely voters surveyed September 19 to September 22. Big Data Poll had Talarico ahead 47 percent to 45 percent from September 24 to September 26, with Libertarian candidate Brown at 8 percent. The Barbara Jordan Public Policy Research and Survey Center found Talarico ahead by one point among 1,800 likely voters surveyed September 15 to September 19. Republican pollster Trafalgar Group also found Talarico ahead by one point, 46 percent to 45 percent, in a mid-September survey. With the exception of the Marist poll, all of the September margins fall within the surveys' margins of error. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Geoffrey Rowland.
news.summary: Some of Texas' wealthiest neighborhoods are giving more to Democrat James Talarico than GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: Stewart expects Schumer, Jeffries to disappoint if the Dems win back the House and Senate
news.text: Talk show host Jon Stewart suggested that even if Democrats win a massive victory in the midterms, a future Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and a future Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., will turn out to be massive disappointments. Democrats were initially in disarray after President Donald Trump’s victory against Kamala Harris in November. However, as Trump’s base fractured amid the Iran war and the affordability crisis that followed, Democrats are expected to win a historic victory in this November’s midterms. On Wednesday, Stewart was asked a humorous question on his podcast about whether the downside of a Democratic midterm victory will be Schumer and Jeffries getting more "airtime." "Look, I think what’s going to happen is they’re going to have to f---ing do something. They’re going to have to deliver," he said. "They’re not going to be able — it will not be sufficient to make their entire personalities opposition to whatever Trump politics are; they’re going to have to have a prescription for rebalancing this economy in a smart and urgent way. JOHNSON DOWNPLAYS GOP'S MIDTERM WOES AS DEMOCRATS EYE HOUSE TAKEOVER: 'I AM VERY BULLISH' "I am not confident that is in their DNA," Stewart continued. "I’m not confident that it’s in Schumer’s DNA, certainly, which means I’m actually hopeful he won’t be there as the leader. That they will come in and say, ‘We’re not going to go down that corporatist path again. We are going to make the changes that the American people are demanding that we make in an urgent way that is not bound by some idealized vision of what the parliamentarian might think is OK.’" "F--- that," Stewart said. "Like, if you are granted control, if they give you the ring, do something with it, you b-----ds." Fox News Digital contacted Jeffries and Schumer and did not receive an immediate reply. HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY' CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Veteran GOP strategist Mary Marslender told Fox News Digital she agrees with Stewart's take."I agree with Jon Stewart that both Schumer and Jeffries are not confident leaders, but that’s because their ideology is power," she responded. "They are not the brakes that will restrain the Democratic Party from pursuing a radical agenda. Instead, they often appease the more radical members of their conference and push the party leftwards on issues like the courts, federal agencies, government spending, progressive prosecutors and immigration whenever they have the votes. "Both men have shown little willingness to challenge the party’s more extreme factions; for example, they have said they will welcome DSA candidates who win primaries into their ‘big tent’ party," she added. "They are not centrists; they follow the prevailing political winds within their party and will implement those policies to hold power even if those policies run counter to what the American people support."Former Democratic advisor Dan Turrentine argued that Stewart's comments express the frustration Democratic voters have with party leaders."Voters are frustrated and angry that neither party is focused on them," he told Fox News Digital. "We are winning because Republicans are losing, not because we are doing things well. The D ‘Majority Makers’ are not going to be the progressive, base candidates, but moderates who will want to focus on commonsense affordability issues, not the 'revenge' and ‘blow everything up’ base stuff. "Jeffries and Schumer will need to balance this to protect their majority while maintaining base enthusiasm. It is a ‘both’ and not ‘either/or’ scenario. Given how weak both are, and that they both will face a primary challenge next year, it is going to be tough. "I think Stewart is indicative of the irrational expectations of the base. They don’t appreciate the different reasons different people are angry. news.summary: Jon Stewart warns Hakeem Jeffries and Schumer must deliver urgent economic results if Democrats win a historic midterm victory this November.

news.title: Joe Scarborough and wife's incredibly awkward clash on air after he scoffs that Democrats are 'so easy to beat' ahead of Midterms
news.text:
Morning Joe host Joe Scarborough took elected Democrats to task on Wednesday, visibly annoying his wife and costar, Mika Brzezinski, in the process.

Scarborough, 63, embarked on the rant roughly an hour into the MS NOW morning show, during a segment about President Donald Trump.

Trump, 80, billed North Korean leader Kim Jong Un as 'a friend' of the US on Tuesday – a statement Scarborough said helped prove his belief that Washington Republicans were unwilling to confront the President with criticism.

The host claimed conservatives would do anything to avoid alienating their 'base' as midterms loom.

Scarborough then suddenly started scolding members of the more progressive party for failing to capitalize.

A visibly unenthused Brzezinski, 59, pleaded for her husband to 'stop' several times during the minute-long missive that ensued. 

'You know, if the Democrats actually- you know, Democrats are uniquely qualified in screwing things up. And then, after they screw things up, they go, "We don't deserve good things,"' Scarborough began, putting on a whiny voice for the impression.

'I mean, I've never seen anything like it before in my life.'

The former Florida congressman confessed that 'the four times [he] ran against Democrats, it was a walk in the park. They're so easy.'

'OK, stop,' Brzezinski said for the first time. 

Scarborough protested: 'No, they're just so easy to beat!'

'Stop!' his spouse hit back, before rolling her eyes.

Brzezinski sat mostly silent, with her eyes squinted, for the rest of Scarborough's rant.

He claimed Democrats have long been 'afraid of their own shadow.'

'And I don't see a whole lot that's changed with Washington Democrats.'

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was minutes away from appearing as a guest. 

With this in mind, Scarborough added: 'There's some great candidates out there, but most of them, they aren't in Washington right now- other than, of course, Hakeem Jeffries, who will be next.'

'Well, talk to him about this,' Brzezinski griped, still oozing distaste.

Scarborough ended the 60-second soapbox by airing his belief that 'if the election goes the way it's looking right now,' Republicans would 'be far more critical' toward opposing candidates. 

'Ok,' Brzezinski said, eager to move on.

'Because they're scared of the base,' Scarborough said.

The next segment followed. 

The dressing-down echoed one offered by the host just last month, where he accused the political party of 'fumbling the football at the two-yard line' as it did in 2025.

'The Democratic Party has a choice to make,' Scarborough said at the time, expressing astonishment at a reluctance from mainstream party members to distance themselves from democratic socialist candidates like Wisconsin state assemblywoman Francesca Hong, who is currently running for governor.

Hong, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, had called for the police to be abolished and for Thanksgiving to be canceled, but has since walked those stances back.

'I said this day-in and day-out leading up to Kamala Harris’ election. You couldn’t watch an NFL game without seeing 300 "Taxpayers are going to pay for trans surgeries for convicts" ads on NFL games,' Scarborough warned.

'Even though [Democrats] still pretend that did not move viewers, I think the Trump campaign spent $30 million on those ads, and it moved working class men, working class white men, working class Black men, working class Hispanic men.

'It just did, and the Democrats had their head in the sand.

'This is not about me,' the former Republican continued. 'This is about the Democrats, once again, fumbling the football on the two-yard line when they have a chance to make great gains, but being… too woke to call out the obvious. 

'I swear to God, it’s really crazy that we’re even having this conversation.
news.summary: Scarborough, 63, embarked on the rant roughly an hour into the MS NOW morning show, during a segment about President Donald Trump.
news.author: Alex Hammer,Editor

news.title: Gavin Newsom claims ‘bull**** artist’ Joe Rogan is too scared to have him join the show
news.text:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has added fuel to his feud with podcaster Joe Rogan, calling him a “bull**** artist” and claiming that he is too scared to have him on his show. 

Rogan, who hosted President Donald Trump shortly before the 2024 election, has repeatedly blasted Newsom on his show, claiming his policies have ruined California. 

When Los Angeles-based YouTuber Shelby Church asked Newsom whether he would appear on popular podcasts like The Joe Rogan Experience and Alex Cooper’s Call Her Daddy, where former Vice President Kamala Harris appeared during her unsuccessful 2024 presidential run against Trump, the governor said Rogan “won’t have me on.”

Newsom said in the interview released this weekend that he has prided himself on “reaching out to the people I disagree with,” mentioning his chats with Fox News host Sean Hannity and the slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk. 

But Newsom claimed Rogan “doesn't want to be confronted with the bull**** he spews, particularly in the political sense. He's a bull**** artist in political terms.”

“I'm happy to confront him, but he won't do it. Now, I'm not even interested because it's been two years of him just bashing me on a weekly basis,” the Democratic governor added. 

Last October, Rogan slammed Newsom on his show amid talks of the governor being a potential candidate for president in 2028. 

“You can’t...ruin a state and say, ‘Guys, that was just practice. Once I get in as president, I’m gonna fix it,’” Rogan said. 

The podcaster called Newsom a “terrible” politician and a “good bull**** artist, claiming that the only reason he’s in office is that he doesn’t have any good competition. 

“You have the highest unemployment. You have the highest homelessness,” Rogan said.

Newsom clapped back at Rogan in an X post at the time, calling him too chicken to have him on his show and “expose his listeners to the truth.” He added that California has the fourth-largest economy in the world and is No. 1 for Fortune 500 companies. 

Rogan doesn’t identify as a Republican or Democrat, but he endorsed Trump in the 2024 election and had him on his show, which is widely viewed among young men. 

The president said during his second inauguration last year that his youngest son, Barron Trump, “knew the youth vote” and told his father, “‘you gotta go out, do Joe Rogan.’”

But Rogan has also criticized Trump on several issues since the president took office, including the war in Iran and a massive immigration crackdown at home. 

Earlier this month, Rogan ripped into Trump for changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” during an escalating trade war with Canada. 

​“It’s to distract you from the fact we are in a war we can’t win with Iran,” Rogan said on his show. “It doesn’t make any sense.”

“Who cares if it’s Lake Ontario? It’s a good name. We’ve had that name forever.”
news.summary: Rogan, who hosted Donald Trump during the 2024 election cycle, has repeatedly criticized the California governor on his podcast, calling him a ‘con man’
news.author: Rachel Dobkin
